---
title: Data Storage
---

All data is stored as JSONL files under `velocirepo/data/`. This entire directory is meant to be committed to git — it's your permanent metric history. Data is organized into three categories:

- `data/metrics/<source>/<project-id>/<date>.jsonl` — time-series metrics (date-partitioned)
- `data/events/<source>/<project-id>/<date>.jsonl` — individual events (date-partitioned)
- `data/content/<source>/<project-id>/<name>.jsonl` — entity data (upsert-by-id)

## Metrics

Sources like PyPI, CRAN, Homebrew, Plausible, OpenVSX, GitHub Traffic, YouTube, and LinkedIn store one JSON object per metric per day:

```json
{"source":"pypi","metric":"daily_downloads","project_id":"plotnine","target":"plotnine","date":"2026-06-15","value":1523}
{"source":"openvsx","metric":"total_downloads","project_id":"quarto","target":"quarto/quarto","date":"2026-06-15","value":1250000}
```

Metric names are prefixed with `daily_` (for deltas — values that reset each day) or `total_` (for snapshots — cumulative totals at a point in time). Homebrew metrics use their own naming (`downloads_30d`, `downloads_365d`, etc.).

`total_*` series are stored only on the days their value changes. Each project's `_watermark.json` records the last day each target was checked, and the `metrics_filled` view fills in the days in between.

Fields:

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `source` | Source name (pypi, cran, homebrew, plausible, openvsx, github-traffic, youtube, linkedin) |
| `metric` | Metric name (e.g., `daily_downloads`, `total_views`, `daily_pageviews`) |
| `project_id` | Project ID from your config |
| `target` | Specific package, repo, site, or extension being tracked |
| `date` | Date of the measurement (YYYY-MM-DD) |
| `value` | Integer value |
| `extra` | Optional key-value metadata (e.g., `{"video_id": "..."}` for YouTube) |

## Events

Event sources store individual events rather than pre-computed counts, giving you full historical detail including who performed each action and when. Currently, GitHub is the only event source.

```json
{"source":"github","type":"fork","project_id":"quarto","target":"quarto-dev/quarto-cli","datetime":"2026-06-15T14:23:01Z","user":"alice"}
{"source":"github","type":"issue_close","project_id":"quarto","target":"quarto-dev/quarto-cli","datetime":"2026-06-15T09:11:44Z","ref":1234,"user":"bob"}
```

Fields:

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `source` | Source name (e.g., `github`) |
| `type` | Event type (e.g., fork, issue_open, issue_close, pr_open, pr_merge, comment) |
| `project_id` | Project ID from your config |
| `target` | Specific repo or resource being tracked (e.g., `owner/repo`) |
| `datetime` | Full timestamp of the event (ISO 8601, UTC) |
| `ref` | Issue or pull request number, for events about one |
| `user` | Who performed the action, if known |
| `extra` | Optional key-value metadata |

These events are automatically aggregated into daily counts in the `metrics` DuckDB view (as `daily_forks`, `daily_issues_opened`, etc.) so you can [query them](querying.qmd) alongside other sources.

Stars aren't events. GitHub only lists the stargazers of repositories your token can administer, so velocirepo reads GitHub's star history instead, which gives the number of stars per day for any repository. It's stored as the `daily_stars` metric. Its days end in US Pacific time, and each fetch re-reads the last 7 days, since stars that are removed again lower the count of their day. The `total_stars` metric holds the star count GitHub reports on each fetch. Star events stored by earlier versions stay in the `events` view, but aren't counted in `daily_stars`.

The star history covers a repository's whole life. To fill in `daily_stars` for data fetched with an earlier version, run `velocirepo fetch-github` once with a `--start-date` before the first star.

## Content

Sources that implement the `ContentProvider` interface also write entity data to `data/content/<source>/<project-id>/<name>.jsonl`. These files use upsert-by-id (new entries are merged with existing ones) rather than date-partitioned concatenation.

YouTube (videos), LinkedIn (posts), RSS (feed items) and GitHub (issues, pull requests and repositories) are content sources. Entries are identified by their target and `id`. YouTube, for example, writes video metadata to `velocirepo/data/content/youtube/<project-id>/videos.jsonl`:

```json
{"source":"youtube","target":"@Fireship","id":"ML3q7Ok4hJg","title":"God-Tier Developer Roadmap","published_at":"2024-03-15T16:00:00Z","duration":423,"tags":["programming","roadmap"]}
```

LinkedIn writes post metadata to `velocirepo/data/content/linkedin/<project-id>/posts.jsonl`. Content is exposed as the `content` DuckDB view; filter by `source` to query source-specific entities.

## Concatenation

After every fetch, daily files are concatenated into monthly files, and monthly files into yearly files, to keep the file count manageable for long-running histories. A month is concatenated once it has ended *and* its last day has been stored. For example, `2026-01.jsonl` is written once data for 31 January 2026 (or a later day) is in place; a year needs 31 December. If the last day is still missing — the fetch failed that night, or the source publishes its data a day late, as CRAN does — the month stays as daily files and the next fetch fills the gap first. The original files are removed after concatenation.

The next fetch resumes the day after the latest stored date, and a monthly or yearly file counts as stored through the last day of its period.

### Backfilling and repairing

Use `--start-date` and `--end-date` to fetch a past range again, for example to backfill a target you just added or to fill a gap:

```bash
velocirepo fetch-cran --start-date 2026-07-31 --end-date 2026-07-31
```

Data for a period that has already been concatenated is merged into its monthly or yearly file. When the same record (same metric, target, date and `extra`) exists twice, the more recently written one wins, so a re-fetch corrects earlier values.

::: {.callout-warning}
Versions of velocirepo before this one replaced a monthly or yearly file with whatever daily files were present. They also concatenated months whose last day was missing, which then never got fetched. Upgrade before backfilling into past months. If a monthly or yearly file shrank after a backfill, restore it from git history.
:::

`velocirepo validate-data` reports daily files next to their month's file, monthly files next to their year's file, and temp files left by interrupted writes. Queries count overlapping data twice until it's merged; `--fix` merges or removes them.

## Migrating data

When a new version of velocirepo changes the on-disk data format, it tracks this with a schema version number in `velocirepo/data/.schema-version`. Commands like `fetch`, `query`, and `export` will refuse to run against stale data:

```
Error: data schema is at version 0, but version 1 is required; run `velocirepo migrate` to update
```

To migrate your data to the latest schema:

```bash
velocirepo migrate
```

Use `--force` to re-run all migrations from scratch:

```bash
velocirepo migrate --force
```

This is safe to run repeatedly — all migrations are idempotent. To merge data from an older schema into a current data directory (e.g., data from another repository), first migrate it in a data directory of its own, then copy the migrated files in. The migrations that move files only look at the old layout, and refuse to merge into directories that already exist.

## Repository layout

You can either keep metrics in the same repository as your code, or create a dedicated metrics repository. A separate repo is useful when you want to track multiple projects in one place or keep metric history out of your main codebase.
